sections.html:
Florence serves as the county seat of Florence County, up in the northeastern coastal plain, at the point where I-20 terminates and I-95 runs past. In 2020 it had 39,899 residents on roughly 23.5 square miles, and 199,630 lived in the metro area. The city grew up at a railroad junction, which explains its street grid and older commercial blocks.

Healthcare is the largest employer base, led by McLeod Regional Medical Center and MUSC Florence, with manufacturing and corporate operations behind it. Buyers therefore come from several workplaces, and a nurse, a plant technician and a university employee may each look at your neighborhood differently. Own a house on an older street near downtown? Buyers will ask how old it is. The Timrod Park area, known for older homes, is part of the downtown redevelopment district.

Hurricane Florence in September 2018 is the storm local buyers remember. The State Climatology Office reports that the Pee Dee River at Pee Dee crested at 31.83 feet, about a foot and a half under its 1945 record. Drought before the storm held the flooding down, but water from North Carolina moved slowly through the Yadkin-Pee Dee watershed, so high water lingered across the region.

July highs average 92.9 degrees, so cooling systems and roofs age fast here. Before you list, assemble the following:

  • Install dates on the roof, heating and cooling system and water heater.
  • Flood or water damage records and repair receipts, kept together.
  • The details of your flood insurance policy, which buyers and lenders will request.
  • Photos of standing water, crawlspace conditions and drainage after a hard rain, if you can take them.

To learn about a specific address, check with the county and your insurer.

Sellers often fear that Florence's flood history will sink the price. History alone rarely does; damage nobody can document often does. A buyer who can read a clean repair history and a current insurance quote has far less to argue about than one who is guessing.

sections.h2: Property tax bills and penalty dates
sections.html:
Real estate tax is billed once a year by Florence County and collected by the County Treasurer. City millage is fixed by June 30 for the fiscal year starting July 1, at $54.90 per $1,000 of assessed value, and county and school levies are layered on.

Homes that qualify as the owner's residence are assessed at 4 percent of market value. Rental and business real property is assessed at 6 percent. Notices from the five-year reappraisal usually go out around May.

DatePenalty
January 15Taxes due (next business day if a weekend or holiday)
January 163 percent
February 2Additional 7 percent, 10 percent total
March 17Additional 5 percent, 15 percent total, plus collection costs

You can reach the Treasurer at 843-665-3041, the Tax Assessor at 843-665-3056 and the delinquent tax office at 843-665-3095. The city's tax payment page explains payment options. The county can auction delinquent real property and mobile homes. Behind on taxes while selling? The balance is paid from your closing proceeds, so request a payoff figure well ahead of time.

sections.h2: The legal steps of a Florence sale
sections.html:
Closings here require a South Carolina attorney. In Boone v. Quicken Loans (2017), the state Supreme Court treated preparing deeds, examining title, overseeing closings and disbursing loan funds as practicing law.

Deeds are filed with the Florence County Register of Deeds at 180 N. Irby Street, 843-665-3032. Staff there record deeds, plats and mortgages, and they leave deed drafting, title searches and legal advice to others. Its county page links a fee sheet and an online search.

The state deed recording fee is $1.85 for realty valued at $100 to $500, plus $1.30 for each additional $500, as the Department of Revenue page shows.

Before a contract is signed, the seller must give the buyer a written property condition disclosure statement, unless the sale is exempt. The state code exempts several kinds of transfer: those made by a fiduciary of an estate, trust or conservatorship, court-ordered sales, gifts to a spouse or lineal relatives, and any sale where both sides agree in writing to skip the form. If something in the form changes before closing, the owner has to correct it or make reasonable repairs.

Permits for building, additions and remodeling come from the city's Building and Permitting Department, 324 West Evans Street. Hours are weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and the number is 843-665-3151. Use the online self-service portal to apply or request an inspection.

The city enforces the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code along with the 2021 residential and building codes. For a vacant house, that means a code officer can cite conditions a buyer would never see in a listing photo. Unpermitted work should be disclosed to a buyer early. Phone the department with your address to see what is on file, and check with them before starting any repair or signing a contract that hinges on a permit.

Florence sellers usually land in one of these groups.

  • Inherited homes: an estate representative generally does not need to give the state disclosure form, yet the deed must still be recorded and an attorney must still run the closing.
  • Rentals: the county taxes rental property at 6 percent instead of 4, so a former occupant should ask the Tax Assessor where any legal residence credit stands.
  • Tax arrears: once the penalty dates above pass, the county may auction unpaid real property.
  • Older homes near downtown: be ready for questions about the roof, wiring and plumbing, and collect permit records.

Cash buyers will take a Florence house as is, though the closing still goes through a South Carolina attorney and the Register of Deeds. Weigh each offer against your likely net after repairs, tax proration and listing time.

As the closing date nears, confirm the payoff on your mortgage, the amount of any tax owed, and who is signing. Bring photo ID and keys. If an heir, a former spouse or a co-owner is on the title, have the attorney review it early so the signature list is complete.

Also decide what stays with the house. Appliances, window coverings and shed contents are easy to argue about, so write down the list and give it to the attorney. A short, clear list heads off an argument over a refrigerator or a backyard shed at the final walkthrough, and it costs you ten minutes of typing. Include garage door remotes, gate codes and any manuals for the HVAC system.

faqs.q: Do I need an attorney to sell a house in Florence, SC?
faqs.a: In practice, yes. Since preparing a deed, examining title and supervising a closing count as practicing law in South Carolina, a South Carolina attorney runs the closing, and the deed is filed with the Florence County Register of Deeds.

faqs.q: When are Florence property taxes due?
faqs.a: January 15 each year, or the next business day if that date falls on a weekend or holiday. Penalties start on January 16 at 3 percent and reach 15 percent after March 17.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Florence County?
faqs.a: Take it to the Register of Deeds, 180 N. Irby Street, Florence, SC 29501 (843-665-3032). The staff file deeds and mortgages, but drafting and legal advice are not part of their job.

faqs.q: Did Hurricane Florence flood the city of Florence?
faqs.a: The 2018 storm caused prolonged river flooding across the Pee Dee region, and the Pee Dee River crested at 31.83 feet at Pee Dee. For one address, ask the county and your insurer.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited house in Florence without a disclosure form?
faqs.a: Often yes. South Carolina exempts transfers by fiduciaries who administer a decedent's estate from the disclosure requirement. Confirm with your closing attorney, because the exemption depends on who signs the deed.
